conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot signs of depression, anxiety, or distress that can creep up after childbirth. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the small team that supports your care, so please answer as openly as feels safe. There are no right or wrong replies—just whatever is true for you today. When you’re ready, we’ll start.  

To begin: Overall, in the past week, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you usually do, or has that felt harder lately?

I still enjoy things, maybe just a little less than before. Like, when my sister visited and we watched a show together, I liked it—but I noticed I wasn’t quite as excited as I used to be. It’s not gone, just… muted.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yes, I’ve still been able to laugh. Just yesterday my partner made a goofy face while changing the baby’s diaper and I burst out giggling. It maybe doesn’t come quite as easily as before, but the funny side is definitely still there.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Yeah, I do look forward to stuff—like our weekly stroller walk with the neighbor moms. It’s not that electric excitement I used to feel, more a quiet “that’ll be nice,” but I still mark it on the calendar and feel good thinking about it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If the baby spits up a lot or won’t settle, I might think, “Maybe I ate something that bothered him,” but the thought passes quickly. I don’t sit there beating myself up—mostly I just move on to the next thing that needs doing.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
I do get little waves of worry, mostly about the baby—like if he’s breathing okay when he’s napping. Nothing huge, just a quick check and I’m fine. It doesn’t feel random; it’s always tied to him.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t had that. I might feel a quick flutter of nerves when he cries suddenly, but it’s not a real panic—just a “hurry-up-and-fix-it” feeling that fades once I figure out what he needs.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah—like when the laundry piles up and he wants to cluster-feed. For a minute it feels like “how will I ever finish anything?” but I take a breath, tackle one small chore, and it passes. I’m keeping my head above water most days.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my sleep’s actually been okay. Once the baby settles for the night, I drift off pretty easily. I’m tired, but it’s more from the night feeds than from feeling unhappy.
I have felt sad or miserable
I’ve had a couple of teary moments—mostly when I’m really tired—but it’s not an all-day sadness. It lifts once I rest or someone gives me a hug.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Only once this week, and it was after a night where the baby woke up every hour. Once I got a short nap, the tears stopped. I haven’t been crying regularly—just that one exhausted moment.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I want to be here for my baby—those thoughts haven’t crossed my mind at all.

You're doing really well in these early weeks, Mum. You shared that you still laugh with your partner, look forward to your neighbourhood stroller walks, and comfort your baby with steady hands-yet you've noticed joy feels <quote>a little muted</quote>, occasional tired tears sneak in, and chores sometimes pile up faster than your energy returns. These ups and downs are common as your body and life adjust, and your honesty helps us keep you supported.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 7, Risk Level: Depression not likely
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map onto core mood, anxiety, guilt, coping, and self-harm domains. A score of 7 places you below the 8-point threshold where <med>postpartum depression</med> screening concern typically begins. You endorsed only mild <sym>anhedonia</sym> (Q1, Q2), rare situational worries (Q4), transient overwhelm (Q6), and tired-related crying (Q8, Q9) while denying persistent low mood, excessive guilt, panic, sleep disruption due to mood, or self-harm thoughts (Q3, Q5, Q7, Q10). This pattern does not meet <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, which requires ≥5 symptoms including depressed mood or anhedonia most of the day, nearly every day, for two weeks. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange routine six-week postpartum check with your <med>primary care provider (PCP)</med>
2. Continue good sleep hygiene: nap when baby naps, share night feeds when possible
3. Keep scheduled social outlets like the weekly stroller walk to reinforce support
4. Re-screen with EPDS in 2-4 weeks or sooner should mood, worry, or crying worsen
5. Contact midwife, health visitor, or <med>mental health specialist</med> promptly if you notice persistent sadness, intrusive thoughts, or any self-harm ideas
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 7: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  

Patient: Postpartum mother (self-report via EPDS-10 items)  
Date: [today]  

Symptoms endorsed  
- Occasional tearfulness when fatigued (Q8, Q9)  
- Transient “getting on top of me” feelings with chore pile-up (Q6)  
- Situational worries about infant safety (Q4)  

Symptoms denied  
- Persistent low mood, pervasive anhedonia, excessive guilt, panic attacks, sleep disturbance secondary to mood, self-harm ideation (Q1, Q3, Q5, Q7, Q10)  

Pattern  
Maintained capacity for pleasure/humor (laughing, looking forward to walks), rapid return to baseline after stressor, no functional impairment beyond normal new-mother fatigue.  No red-flag signs for major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder on this screen.  Continue routine postpartum follow-up; re-screen if symptoms worsen or persist >2 weeks.
